text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The murder of Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme could be solved after a statement by deceased Lars Tingstrom, nicknamed the Bomb Man, came out into the open. Tingstrom's lawyer Pelle Svensson indicated that Christer Pettersson, once convicted but then acquitted of the murder, was among a group of four people involved in the 1986 murder.

- Support is growing to bring Mona Sahlin back into the ruling Social Democrats government ahead of the September 1998 general election. Sahlin, once destined to lead the party, stepped down from the government amid a controversy over her using work credit cards to temporary cover personal expenses.

- Volvo board member Hakan Frisinger is set to take over the chairmanship of the company following the death of Bert-Olof Svanholm on Tuesday. Frisinger has been appointed acting chairman until Volvo's annual general meeting on April 23 when he will be proposed to take the position permanently.

- Sweden's King Carl Gustaf should have been murdered before Prime Minister Olof Palme, according to statement by deceased Lars Tingstrom, the so-called Bomb Man, that has been handed over to the commission investigating Palme's 1986 murder. The statement also said Christer Pettersson, once convicted but then acquitted of the murder, was involved with Tingstrom giving the orders for the murder.

- Former Finance Minister Kjell-Olof Feldt warned over raising taxes and said he was not surprised that the opinion polls have swung against the ruling Social Democratic party. He said changes and cuts had been too severe and a lot of people were now under tight economic pressure.

- Swedish vehicle maker Volvo will pay a premium of 40 crowns over the bourse price in a share redemption programme to redeem about five percent of its shares. The offer will run from May 13 to June 6.
- Irish airline Ryanair is starting to fly from London to Stockholm at cut price fare this June, adding more competition to SAS and British Airways. Ryanair is offering a no frills, cheap service.

- Construction company NCC is expected to land a Polish order worth nearly four billion crowns. NCC is part of a consortium which has been granted a concession to build a four-lane, 362 kms highway between the Polish/German border and the Polish city of Lodz, according to newspaper sources.

- Construction group Skanska and its Finnish subsidiary have landed an order valued at $230 million for what is described as the first privately financed highway in the Nordic region. Skanska will build a 70 kms stretch of highway between Helsinki and the ski resort of Lahti.

- Combitech Traffic System owned by Investor AB has obtained a breakthrough order worth 200-300 million crowns for its automatic highway toll collection system. Trans-Link of Australia will introduce the Combitech system on a highway near Melbourne. It replaces the usual way of paying tolls, allowing for a freer flow of traffic. Commuters carry a wallet-sized transmitter above their dashboard which registers each use of the toll highway.

- Sweden's largest listed companies will pay out 31 billion corwns to sharesholders in dividends this year but some 400,000 Swedish families subject to wealth tax may have to hand over more than 100 percent of the dividends' value to the taxman. The tax bite will be larger than the dividend value if the company share in question has a dividend yield of less than 2.1 percent on December 1977, according to Price Waterhouse tax experts.
